claims.evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq profiles.

claims.claim: The removal of seven parS sites substantially reduced the hyper-enrichment of Smc-CC425 near the origin and increased the signal on the chromosome arms.
claims.source: Remarkably, the removal of seven parS sites substantially reduced the hyper-enrichment near the origin and increased the otherwise relatively low signal on the chromosome arms (Figure 2A, B, right panels, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq profiles.

claims.claim: The hyper-enrichment of Smc in the replication origin region correlated with poor chromosome arm alignment.
claims.source: The hyper-enrichment of Smc in the replication origin region thus correlated with poor chromosome arm alignment (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This correlation is observed by comparing ChIP-seq and 3C-seq data.

claims.claim: In the presence of multiple parS sites, the modified Smc coiled coil either impedes Smc translocation provoking frequent collisions and unproductive loop formation or increases the rate of unloading and subsequent reloading events in the origin region.
claims.source: These results suggest that in the presence of multiple parS sites the modified Smc coiled coil either impedes Smc translocation provoking frequent collisions and unproductive loop formation or increases the rate of unloading and subsequent reloading events in the origin region.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the ChIP-seq and 3C-seq data.

claims.claim: Both impediment of Smc translocation and increased unloading/reloading could explain the hyper-enrichment of Smc-CC425 in the origin region.
claims.source: Both hypotheses could equally well explain the hyper-enrichment of Smc-CC425 in that region.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about possible mechanisms.

claims.claim: Smc and Smc-CC425 complexes were both enriched in an ~700 kb region centered on the replication origin after 20 min of ParB induction.
claims.source: Smc and Smc-CC425 complexes were both found enriched in an ~700 kb region centered on the replication origin after 20 min of ParB induction by ChIP-seq analysis using α-ScpB serum (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq time-course experiments.

claims.claim: For wild-type Smc, the enriched region increased in size over time, inferring a constant DNA translocation rate of roughly 500 bp/s at 30°C.
claims.source: For wild-type Smc, the enriched region increased in size over time, inferring a constant DNA translocation rate of roughly 500 bp/s at 30°C.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from ChIP-seq time-course data.

claims.claim: The high enrichment of wild-type Smc near parS disappeared at later time points as Smc-ScpAB became more broadly distributed on the chromosome.
claims.source: Notably, the high enrichment near parS disappeared at the later time points as Smc-ScpAB became more broadly distributed on the chromosome.
claims.evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq time-course experiments.

claims.claim: The region of Smc-CC425 enrichment broadened during later time intervals, albeit with an apparently reducing rate.
claims.source: The region of Smc-ScpAB enrichment also broadened in Smc-CC425 during the later time intervals, albeit with an apparently reducing rate.
claims.evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq time-course experiments.

claims.claim: The origin region remained highly enriched in ScpB at later time points in Smc-CC425.
claims.source: In addition, the origin region remained highly enriched in ScpB also at the later time points.
claims.evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq time-course experiments.

claims.claim: Smc-CC425 was able to align chromosome arms in the ParB depletion/repletion experimental system, yet the alignment did not extend all the way to the ter region.
claims.source: Using 3C-seq, we observed that Smc-CC425 was able to align chromosome arms in this experimental system, yet the alignment did not extend all the way to the ter region (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq time-course experiments.

claims.claim: The onset of chromosome alignment and the rate of progress appeared somewhat reduced for Smc-CC425 when compared to wild-type Smc.
claims.source: Moreover, the onset of chromosome alignment as well as the rate of progress appeared somewhat reduced when compared to wild-type Smc.
claims.evidence: This is observed by comparing 3C-seq time-course data.

claims.claim: The translocation rates of Smc-CC425 appeared to reduce at later time points, possibly due to increased spontaneous unloading.
claims.source: Moreover, the translocation rates appeared to reduce at later timer points, possibly due to increased spontaneous unloading of Smc-CC425.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from ChIP-seq and 3C-seq time-course data.

claims.claim: Smc-CC425 efficiently accumulated in the replication origin region, but translocation to distal loci on the chromosome arms was hampered.
claims.source: Regardless, these experiments demonstrate that Smc-CC425 efficiently accumulated in the replication origin region, but the translocation to distal loci on the chromosome arms was hampered.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from ChIP-seq and 3C-seq time-course experiments.

claims.claim: A simple explanation for the hyper-accumulation of Smc-CC425 in the replication origin region is an increase in spontaneous unloading of translocating Smc.
claims.source: A simple explanation for the hyper-accumulation of Smc-CC425 in the replication origin region (in the presence of a single parS site) is an increase in spontaneous unloading of translocating Smc.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanistic explanation.

claims.claim: Shorter periods of time spent translocating along chromosome arms increases the cytoplasmic pool of Smc and consequently the flux of loading.
claims.source: With shorter periods of time spent translocating along the chromosome arms, the cytoplasmic pool of Smc increases and as a consequence so does the flux of loading, which—possibly together with a reduced translocation rate—leads to artificially increased enrichment near the parS site(s).
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between residency time and loading flux.

claims.claim: Increased loading flux leads to artificially increased enrichment near parS sites.
claims.source: With shorter periods of time spent translocating along the chromosome arms, the cytoplasmic pool of Smc increases and as a consequence so does the flux of loading, which—possibly together with a reduced translocation rate—leads to artificially increased enrichment near the parS site(s).
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of increased loading.

claims.claim: Smc collisions would further exacerbate the Smc hyper-enrichment by hindering Smc translocation away from parS sites.
claims.source: Such collisions would further exacerbate the Smc hyper-enrichment by hindering Smc translocation away from parS sites (Figure 2A, right panel).
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of collisions.

claims.claim: A reduced chromosome residency time and a reduced translocation rate may explain all phenotypic consequences of the Smc arm-modifications.
claims.source: A reduced chromosome residency time and a reduced translocation rate may thus explain all phenotypic consequences of the Smc arm-modifications.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed unified explanation for the observed phenotypes.

claims.claim: Wild-type Smc displayed relatively low enrichment in the replication origin region even when all natural parS sites were present.
claims.source: Wild-type Smc displayed relatively low enrichment in the replication origin region even when all natural parS sites were present (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq profiles.

claims.claim: Control strains with a unique parSopt sequence at positions −9 kb, −304 kb, or +328 kb demonstrated extensive alignment of the respective flanking regions.
claims.source: As expected, control strains with a unique parSopt sequence at positions −9 kb, at −304 kb, or at +328 kb (at amyE) demonstrated extensive alignment of the respective flanking regions (Figure 3A; Wang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps and is consistent with cited literature.

claims.claim: The +328kbparSopt site, and to a lesser extent the –304kbparSopt site, resulted in asymmetric alignment of the flanking DNA probably due to the presence of clusters of highly transcribed genes in head-on orientation.
claims.source: The +328kbparSopt site, and to a lesser extent the –304kbparSopt site, resulted in asymmetric alignment of the flanking DNA probably due to the presence of clusters of highly transcribed genes (including rDNA operons) in head-on orientation (Brandão et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq maps and explained by cited work on transcription effects.

claims.claim: The frequency of contacts reaching beyond the replication origin is notably reduced with –304kbparSopt or +328kbparSopt, implying that the origin region acts as a semi-permissive barrier for Smc translocation.
claims.source: Of note, the frequency of contacts reaching beyond the replication origin is notably reduced with –304kbparSopt or +328kbparSopt, implying that the origin region acts as a semi-permissive barrier for Smc translocation (or a Smc unloading site), as previously noted (Minnen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq maps and is consistent with cited literature.

claims.claim: When two parS sites were combined on the chromosome, striking novel patterns of chromosome organization by wild-type Smc arose.
claims.source: More importantly, when two parS sites were combined on the chromosome, striking novel patterns of chromosome organization by wild-type Smc arose (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps.

claims.claim: Parallel secondary diagonals emerging from the two parS sites were detected when two parS sites were combined.
claims.source: In all cases, parallel secondary diagonals emerging from the two parS sites were detected.
claims.evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps.

claims.claim: The pattern observed with –304kbparSopt and –9kbparSopt can largely be explained as a combination of contacts observed in strains with the corresponding single parS sites, with clearly reduced probability for contacts extending beyond the region demarcated by the parS sites.
claims.source: The pattern observed with –304kbparSopt and –9kbparSopt can—to a large degree—be explained as a combination of contacts observed in strains with the corresponding single parS sites, however, with clearly reduced probability for contacts extending beyond the region demarcated by the parS sites.
claims.evidence: This is observed by comparing 3C-seq contact maps.

claims.claim: A small but noticeable fraction of Smc complexes managed to translocate towards and beyond the other parS site mostly unhindered.
claims.source: A small but noticeable fraction of Smc complexes however apparently managed to translocate towards and beyond the other parS site mostly unhindered (as indicated by the largely unaltered position of the secondary diagonals).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the presence of secondary diagonals in 3C-seq maps.

claims.claim: Treatment with rifampicin did not significantly alter the contact pattern with two parS sites apart from generating noisier maps.
claims.source: Treatment with rif did not significantly alter the contact pattern (apart from generating noisier maps) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq experiments with rifampicin treatment.

claims.claim: The contact maps involving the –304kbparSopt and +328kbparSopt sites showed additional contacts likely representing paired loops originating from collided Smc complexes loaded at opposite parS sites.
claims.source: The contact maps involving the –304kbparSopt and +328kbparSopt sites showed additional contacts likely representing paired loops originating from collided Smc complexes loaded at opposite parS sites (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps and interpreted based on the experimental design.

claims.claim: Wild-type Smc-ScpAB complexes rarely block one another when loaded from all natural parS sites with the notable exception of –304kbparS.
claims.source: We conclude that wild-type Smc-ScpAB complexes rarely block one another when loaded from all natural parS sites (with the notable exception of –304kbparS).
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the relatively normal 3C-seq patterns with all natural parS sites.

claims.claim: When the distance between two strong parS sites was artificially increased, impacts arising from collisions and blockage became noticeable.
claims.source: When the distance between two strong parS sites was artificially increased, however, impacts arising from collisions and blockage became noticeable.
claims.evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq maps with repositioned parS sites.

claims.claim: The blockage of Smc translocation was apparent from ChIP-seq analysis showing hyper-enrichment of Smc between two parS sites when compared to the single parS control.
claims.source: The blockage of Smc translocation was also apparent from ChIP-seq analysis, which demonstrated hyper-enrichment of Smc between two parS sites (–304kbparSopt and –9kbparSopt or –9kbparSopt and +328kbparSopt) when compared to the single parS control (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D).
claims.evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq profiles.

claims.claim: The effects of collisions on chromosome organization and Smc distribution are subdued with wild-type Smc but readily detectable upon repositioning of parS sites.
claims.source: The effects of collisions on chromosome organization and Smc distribution are thus subdued with wild-type Smc but readily detectable upon repositioning of parS sites.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from comparing different parS configurations.

claims.claim: If Smc-CC425 fails to juxtapose chromosome arms due to an increased flux in the replication origin region, collisions may be rare in wild-type cells because of a high chromosome residency time and a limited pool of soluble Smc complexes, resulting in a low flux of Smc onto the chromosome.
claims.source: If Smc-CC425 indeed fails to juxtapose chromosome arms due to an increased flux in the replication origin region, collisions may be rare in wild-type cells because of a high chromosome residency time and a limited pool of soluble Smc complexes, resulting in a low flux of Smc onto the chromosome.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference connecting the observations with Smc-CC425 to wild-type behavior.

claims.claim: Artificially increasing the flux of Smc should lead to defects in chromosome organization with multiple parS sites but not with a single parS site if collisions are rare due to low flux.
claims.source: If so, artificially increasing the flux of Smc should lead to defects in chromosome organization with multiple parS sites but not with a single parS site (as observed for Smc-CC425 under normal expression levels) (assuming that most Smc is loaded at parS).
claims.evidence: This is a testable prediction based on the collision avoidance hypothesis.

claims.claim: If Smc complexes efficiently traverse, reverse, or unload one another, then increased Smc levels would not result in defective translocation and chromosome organization.
claims.source: If Smc complexes, however, were to efficiently traverse, reverse, or unload one another, then increased Smc levels would not result in defective translocation and chromosome organization.
claims.evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis that can be tested.

claims.claim: Immunoblotting suggested a four- to fivefold increase in Smc and ScpB protein levels in the SMChigh strain when compared to wild type.
claims.source: Immunoblotting suggested a four- to fivefold increase in Smc and ScpB protein levels in the SMChigh strain when compared to wild type (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting experiments.

claims.claim: Chromosome arm co-alignment was strongly hampered by the presence of extra Smc complexes in the cell.
claims.source: Chromosome arm co-alignment was strongly hampered—rather than improved—by the presence of extra Smc complexes in the cell (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps of SMChigh strains.

claims.claim: A prominent arc was formed at the position of the –304kbparS site in the SMChigh strain.
claims.source: A prominent arc was formed at the position of the –304kbparS site, and the secondary diagonal originating in the origin region was weak and diffuse in the SMChigh strain.
claims.evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps.

claims.claim: The defect in chromosome organization in SMChigh was fully restored by removal of seven parS sites.
claims.source: This defect was fully restored, however, by removal of seven parS sites (with the remaining strong site being either –9kbparSopt or –304kbparSopt) (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps.

claims.claim: An additional minor secondary diagonal present on the right arm of the chromosome in SMChigh likely originated from Smc loading at the weak +1058kbparS site.
claims.source: Note that an additional feature (a minor secondary diagonal) present on the right arm of the chromosome likely originated from Smc loading at the weak +1058kbparS site.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the position of the feature and knowledge of parS sites.

claims.claim: The presence of two strong parS sites led to a new pattern of chromosome folding in the SMChigh strain with highly asymmetric alignment of DNA flanking the parS sites.
claims.source: The presence of two strong parS sites (–9kbparSopt and –304kbparSopt) led to a new pattern of chromosome folding in the SMChigh strain. The alignment of DNA flanking the parS sites became highly asymmetric, presumably because Smc complexes loaded at opposite parS sites hinder each other (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps.

claims.claim: Contacts corresponding to paired loops became clearly visible in SMChigh with two parS sites.
claims.source: Moreover, the contacts corresponding to paired loops became clearly visible (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps.

claims.claim: Contacts outside the parS-demarcated region were rare and spread out in SMChigh with two parS sites, and their center was shifted away from the parS sites.
claims.source: Finally, contacts outside the parS-demarcated region were rare and spread out, and their center was shifted away from the parS sites.
claims.evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps.

claims.claim: Only a few Smc complexes loaded at one parS site managed to move beyond the other parS site in SMChigh.
claims.source: The former indicated that only a few Smc complexes loaded at one parS site managed to move beyond the other parS site.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of contacts in 3C-seq maps.

claims.claim: Smc complexes that moved from one parS site to the other experienced a strongly reduced translocation rate, presumably due to encounters with Smc complexes translocating in opposite orientation.
claims.source: And if they did, they experienced a strongly reduced translocation rate when moving from parS site to the other, presumably due to encounters with and temporary (or partial) blockage by Smc complexes translocating in opposite orientation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the shifted center of contacts in 3C-seq maps.

claims.claim: The hindrance observed with two or all parS sites in SMChigh was not relieved by treatment with rifampicin, being consistent with Smc-Smc encounters rather than Smc-RNA polymerase encounters being mainly responsible.
claims.source: Importantly, the hindrance observed with two or all parS sites being present was not relieved by treatment with rif, being consistent with the notion that Smc-Smc encounters rather than Smc-RNA polymerase encounters are mainly responsible for the impediment of translocation in SMChigh (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq experiments with rifampicin treatment.

claims.claim: The localization of ParB to parS sites is largely unaffected by increased levels of Smc.
claims.source: The α-ParB ChIP-seq demonstrated that the localization of ParB to parS sites is, as expected, largely unaffected by the increased levels of Smc (Figure 4E; Minnen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq experiments.

claims.claim: The chromosomal distribution of ScpB was largely unaffected in SMChigh cells harboring a single –9kbparSopt site.
claims.source: The chromosomal distribution of ScpB was also largely unaffected in SMChigh cells harboring a single –9kbparSopt site (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq profiles.

claims.claim: In the presence of two or multiple additional parS sites, the enrichment of ScpB between the parS sites increased strongly in SMChigh.
claims.source: However, in the presence of two or multiple additional parS sites, the enrichment between the parS sites increased strongly (Figure 4E, F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
claims.evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq profiles.

claims.claim: The changes in ScpB distribution upon parS site removal are remarkably similar in Smc-CC425 and SMChigh.
claims.source: The changes in ScpB distribution upon parS site removal are remarkably similar in Smc-CC425 and SMChigh (compare Figures 2B and 4E), supporting the notion that both modifications lead to more frequent blockage after collisions probably by the same mechanism: an increased flux of Smc in the vicinity of parS sites.
claims.evidence: This is concluded by comparing ChIP-seq data from different experiments.

claims.claim: Both Smc-CC425 and SMChigh modifications lead to more frequent blockage after collisions probably by the same mechanism: an increased flux of Smc in the vicinity of parS sites.
claims.source: The changes in ScpB distribution upon parS site removal are remarkably similar in Smc-CC425 and SMChigh (compare Figures 2B and 4E), supporting the notion that both modifications lead to more frequent blockage after collisions probably by the same mechanism: an increased flux of Smc in the vicinity of parS sites.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the similar phenotypes.

claims.claim: The alignment of DNA starting from –9kbparSopt site was hampered when a second parS site (–304kbparSopt) was present in synchronized loading experiments.
claims.source: We found that the alignment of DNA starting from –9kbparSopt site was indeed hampered when a second parS site, –304kbparSopt, was present (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), even more so than with continuous ParB expression (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq experiments with synchronized ParB induction.

claims.claim: Under physiological conditions, collisions between Smc-ScpAB complexes are kept at a tolerable level by a low cellular abundance of Smc-ScpAB (~30 Smc dimers per chromosome or less), a high DNA translocation rate, an extended time of residency on the chromosome arms, and the preferential usage of a cluster of parS sites.
claims.source: Under physiological conditions, collisions between Smc-ScpAB complexes are kept at a tolerable level by a low cellular abundance of Smc-ScpAB ~30 Smc dimers per chromosome or less (Wilhelm et al., 2015), a high DNA translocation rate, an extended time of residency on the chromosome arms, and the preferential usage of a cluster of parS sites (spanning ~60 kb region of the genome: –68kbparS, –63kbparS, –49kbparS, –9kbparS).
claims.evidence: This is concluded from all the experimental observations and cited literature.

claims.claim: Multiple parameters are fine-tuned to avoid Smc encounters, possibly rendering the resolution of Smc collisions unnecessary.
claims.source: Thus, multiple parameters are fine-tuned to avoid Smc encounters, possibly rendering the resolution of Smc collisions unnecessary.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the overall findings of the study.

claims.claim: Occasional loading of Smc at one of the more distal parS sites would quite often lead to collisions, resulting in contact maps with an arc-shaped pattern.
claims.source: Occasional loading of Smc at one of the more distal parS sites however would quite often lead to collisions, thus resulting in contact maps with an arc-shaped pattern, such as observed for –304kbparS (the strongest of the distal parS sites) (Figure 1C; Brandão et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq maps and consistent with cited modeling work.

claims.claim: The obvious defects in chromosome organization observed with altered parS positioning, elevated Smc levels, or engineered Smc proteins do not substantially impact bacterial growth.
claims.source: The obvious defects in chromosome organization observed with altered parS positioning, elevated Smc levels, or engineered Smc proteins, however, do not substantially impact bacterial growth, suggesting that chromosome segregation is efficiently supported even with Smc collisions (and without chromosome arm alignment being detectable by population-averaging 3C methodology).
claims.evidence: This is observed from growth assays showing normal or near-normal growth.

claims.claim: Chromosome segregation is efficiently supported even with Smc collisions and without detectable chromosome arm alignment by 3C methodology.
claims.source: The obvious defects in chromosome organization observed with altered parS positioning, elevated Smc levels, or engineered Smc proteins, however, do not substantially impact bacterial growth, suggesting that chromosome segregation is efficiently supported even with Smc collisions (and without chromosome arm alignment being detectable by population-averaging 3C methodology).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation of normal growth despite organizational defects.

claims.claim: Colliding Smc complexes might efficiently promote DNA disentanglement locally but hamper the global chromosome folding process.
claims.source: Colliding Smc complexes might thus efficiently promote DNA disentanglement locally (with the help of DNA topoisomerases) but hamper the global chromosome folding process, possibly leading to large cell-to-cell variations in chromosome organization with likely knock-on effects on other cellular processes including nucleoid occlusion and cell division.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional consequences of collisions.

claims.claim: The presence of multiple types of SMC complexes acting on the same chromosome likely aggravates the issue of collisions.
claims.source: The presence of multiple types of SMC complexes acting on the same chromosome likely aggravates the issue of collisions.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference based on the collision problem.

claims.claim: In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Smc-ScpAB appears to limit the loop extrusion activity of MksBEF but not vice versa.
claims.source: In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, the impact of collisions seems to be dealt with by a hierarchy amongst two endogenous SMC complexes and a coordination of SMC activity with chromosome replication (Lioy et al., 2020). Smc-ScpAB appears to limit the loop extrusion activity of MksBEF but not vice versa.
claims.evidence: This is based on a cited study of P. aeruginosa.

claims.claim: When the heterologous E. coli MukBEF complex was introduced in P. aeruginosa in place of MksBEF, it blocked the activity of P. aeruginosa Smc-ScpAB but not the other way around.
claims.source: When the heterologous Escherichia coli MukBEF complex was introduced in place of MksBEF, it blocked the activity of P. aeruginosa Smc-ScpAB but not the other way around.
claims.evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claims.claim: The hierarchy between SMC complexes is possibly given by the relative abundance of these complexes and differing chromosome association dynamics (residency times).
claims.source: The hierarchy is possibly given by the relative abundance of these complexes and differing chromosome association dynamics (residency times).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed hierarchy.

claims.claim: The parsimonious explanation for the observations is that neither wild-type nor modified Smc proteins are able to traverse one another.
claims.source: The parsimonious explanation for our observations—not requiring the involvement of dedicated and potentially hazardous molecular transactions—is that neither wild-type nor modified Smc proteins are able to traverse one another.
claims.evidence: This is proposed as the simplest explanation for the data.

claims.claim: A recent study suggested that Smc traversal is needed to accurately recapitulate the relative abundance of long-range contacts observed with natural and artificial arrangements of parS sites.
claims.source: A recent study describing Smc action in B. subtilis by simulations, however, suggested that Smc traversal is needed to accurately recapitulate the relative abundance of long-range contacts observed with natural and artificial arrangements of parS sites (similar to Figure 3B; Brandão et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on a cited modeling study.

claims.claim: Direct observation of Smc traversal and of interlocking DNA loops (Z loops) on the bacterial chromosome is lacking.
claims.source: Furthermore, direct observation of Smc traversal and of interlocking DNA loops (Z loops) on the bacterial chromosome is lacking.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current state of experimental evidence.

claims.claim: A basic understanding of the molecular transactions necessary for Smc traversal is elusive.
claims.source: Also, a basic understanding of the necessary molecular transactions is elusive.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current state of mechanistic understanding.

claims.claim: A putative defect in traversal might contribute to the hyper-accumulation of Smc-CC425 in the replication origin region and the defective chromosome organization with multiple parS sites.
claims.source: Nevertheless, the idea of Smc traversal is an intriguing proposition with potentially wide implications warranting serious consideration. A putative defect in traversal might contribute to the hyper-accumulation of Smc-CC425 in the replication origin region and the defective chromosome organization with multiple parS sites.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the observations.

claims.claim: The nature and integrity of the Smc hinge domain and the adjacent coiled coil might be critical for the putative bypassing step in Smc traversal.
claims.source: Assuming the validity of Smc traversal, it is tempting to speculate—on the basis of the observations with Smc-CC425—that the nature and the integrity of the Smc hinge domain and the adjacent coiled coil are critical for the putative bypassing step.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the Smc-CC425 phenotype.

claims.claim: How Smc traversal might occur without the risk of establishing unwanted trans DNA linkages is totally unclear.
claims.source: How Smc traversal might occur without the risk of establishing unwanted ('trans') DNA linkages yet is totally unclear.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about a major mechanistic challenge.

claims.claim: The presence of multiple parS sites likely improves the robustness of the chromosome segregation process.
claims.source: The presence of multiple parS sites likely improves the robustness of the chromosome segregation process (Böhm et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claims.claim: Most bacteria have clustered parS sites within a 5–40 kb region and are sensitive to deleting or dispositioning them outside a tolerance region.
claims.source: Most bacteria have clustered parS sites (within 5–40 kb region) and are sensitive to deleting or dispositioning them outside a tolerance region (Böhm et al., 2020; Lagage et al., 2016; Minnen et al., 2011; Tran et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is based on cited studies of parS distribution and function.

claims.claim: Severe consequences of manipulating parS distribution include a longer generation time, an increased number of anucleate cells, and elongated cells.
claims.source: Severe consequences of manipulating parS distribution include a longer generation time (when mksBEF is missing) (Lagage et al., 2016), an increased number of anucleate cells (Böhm et al., 2020) and elongated cells (Tran et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is based on cited studies.

claims.claim: In Caulobacter crescentus, Smc translocates only ~600 kb away from parS.
claims.source: In Caulobacter crescentus, Smc translocates only ~600 kb away from parS (Tran et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claims.claim: The partial chromosome arm alignment in C. crescentus is reminiscent of the observation with modified Smc proteins in B. subtilis.
claims.source: The partial chromosome arm alignment in C. crescentus is reminiscent of the observation with modified Smc proteins in B. subtilis.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison drawn between different organisms.

claims.claim: A shorter chromosome residency time or a lower translocation rate of Smc-ScpAB is acceptable when parS sites are tightly clustered or when combined with a single parS site.
claims.source: It is tempting to speculate that a shorter chromosome residency time or a lower translocation rate of Smc-ScpAB is acceptable when parS sites are tightly clustered or when combined with a single parS site.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting different observations.

claims.claim: Some bacterial genomes harbor multiple parS sites that are quite widely scattered on the genome.
claims.source: Nevertheless, some bacterial genomes harbor multiple parS sites that are quite widely scattered on the genome.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about bacterial genome organization.

claims.claim: The scattered parS distribution is restricted to few lineages on the phylogenetic tree of bacteria, including Bacilli.
claims.source: Intriguingly, the scattered parS distribution is restricted to few lineages on the phylogenetic tree of bacteria, including Bacilli (Livny et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is based on a cited genomic survey.

claims.claim: The scattering of parS sites likely serves a dedicated purpose in the lifestyles of bacteria with scattered parS sites, in B. subtilis possibly during sporulation.
claims.source: The scattering of parS sites likely serves a dedicated purpose in the lifestyles of these bacteria, in B. subtilis possibly during sporulation when large chunks of the genome (~1 Mb, i.e., about a quarter of the genome) are captured at the cell pole to promote entrapment of the chromosome in the pre-spore (Wu and Errington, 1998).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on cited work on sporulation.

claims.claim: Chromosome capture during sporulation might benefit from the condensation of the replication origin involving Smc collisions rather than an alignment of chromosome arms.
claims.source: This process might benefit from the condensation of the replication origin (possibly involving Smc collisions as observed here) rather than an alignment of chromosome arms.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative functional interpretation.

claims.claim: Chromosome arm alignment is lost when DNA replication is artificially blocked and replaced by smaller loops formed at individual parS sites.
claims.source: Consistent with this notion, chromosome arm alignment is lost when DNA replication is artificially blocked (as naturally occurring during sporulation) and replaced by smaller loops formed at individual parS sites (Marbouty et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is based on cited studies.

claims.claim: A simple explanation for the altered pattern of chromosome folding during replication blockage is an increased rate of Smc collisions due to an elevated protein-to-DNA ratio.
claims.source: A simple explanation for this altered pattern of chromosome folding during replication blockage (and possibly also during sporulation) would be an increased rate of Smc collisions due to an elevated (Smc) protein-to-DNA ratio.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanistic explanation.

claims.claim: The process of Smc DNA translocation is finely tuned to keep the probability of Smc encounters at a low level, presumably to enable extensive DNA loop extrusion without the need to resolve Smc collisions.
claims.source: Altogether, our results strongly suggest that the process of Smc DNA translocation is finely tuned to keep the probability of Smc encounters at a low level, presumably to enable extensive DNA loop extrusion without the need to resolve Smc collisions.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental observations.

results.result: Engineered Smc variants with modified coiled coil arm lengths (elongated Smc-CC425 and shortened Smc-CC253) support normal bacterial growth but fail to properly co-align chromosome arms, as demonstrated by 3C-seq analysis showing absence or reduction of secondary diagonals in contact maps.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C40 collectively demonstrate through growth assays, protein expression analysis, chromosome co-entrapment assays, and 3C-seq contact maps that arm-modified Smc variants are expressed at comparable levels to wild-type, assemble into functional complexes, support growth, but fail to organize chromosomes normally. The data directly supports the conclusion that arm modifications specifically impair chromosome organization while maintaining viability.

results.result: Removal of seven parS sites, leaving only a single strong parS site, rescues chromosome arm alignment by modified Smc proteins, while the presence of two or more parS sites hampers chromosome organization, suggesting that multiple loading sites increase Smc collisions.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C55 are well-supported by 3C-seq data showing improved chromosome arm alignment when seven parS sites are removed in strains with modified Smc proteins. The data with single versus multiple parS sites, combined with rifampicin experiments showing partial relief of defects, provide converging evidence that multiple parS sites lead to increased collisions. The mechanistic interpretation is reasonable given the experimental observations.

results.result: Smc-CC425 shows hyper-enrichment near the replication origin and poor distribution toward chromosome arms in ChIP-seq analysis, which correlates with defective chromosome arm alignment. Removal of seven parS sites reduces this hyper-enrichment and improves arm distribution.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C63 are supported by ChIP-seq data showing distinct distribution patterns for wild-type versus Smc-CC425, with clear correlation between hyper-enrichment at the origin and poor chromosome organization. The proposed mechanisms (impediment of translocation or increased unloading/reloading) are reasonable interpretations of the data, though they remain somewhat speculative as alternative explanations are not fully excluded.

results.result: Time-course ChIP-seq and 3C-seq experiments following synchronized ParB induction show that wild-type Smc translocates at ~500 bp/s at 30°C with progressive chromosome arm alignment, while Smc-CC425 shows reduced translocation rates and incomplete arm alignment that does not extend to the terminus region.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C72 are supported by time-course ChIP-seq and 3C-seq data showing differential dynamics between wild-type and Smc-CC425. The calculated translocation rate for wild-type Smc is derived from the data, though the authors acknowledge difficulty in precisely determining rates for Smc-CC425. The conclusion that Smc-CC425 accumulates efficiently at the origin but has hampered translocation to distal loci is well-supported by the experimental observations.

results.result: The hyper-accumulation of Smc-CC425 in the replication origin region is explained by increased spontaneous unloading of translocating Smc, which increases the cytoplasmic pool and loading flux, with collisions further exacerbating the enrichment by hindering translocation away from parS sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C78 present a mechanistic model to explain the observed phenotypes, but this remains largely speculative. While the model is logically consistent with the data, alternative mechanisms are not rigorously excluded. The claims represent reasonable inferences but lack direct experimental validation of the proposed increased unloading or altered loading flux. Additional experiments would be needed to definitively establish this mechanism.

results.result: Wild-type Smc generates overlapping chromosome folding patterns when loaded from two repositioned parS sites, with parallel secondary diagonals and reduced contacts beyond the parS-demarcated region. ChIP-seq shows hyper-enrichment of Smc between two parS sites, indicating blockage of translocation due to collisions.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C92 are well-supported by 3C-seq and ChIP-seq data with engineered parS site positions. The observation of parallel secondary diagonals, reduced long-range contacts, and hyper-enrichment between parS sites provides strong evidence for collision-induced blockage. The rifampicin experiments help distinguish Smc-Smc collisions from Smc-RNA polymerase encounters. The conclusion that wild-type Smc rarely blocks when loaded from natural parS sites but shows detectable collision effects with repositioned sites is well-justified.

results.result: The authors propose that collisions are rare in wild-type cells due to high chromosome residency time and limited soluble Smc pool, predicting that artificially increasing Smc flux should cause defects with multiple but not single parS sites, while efficient traversal/reversal/unloading would prevent such defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C95 present testable predictions based on the collision avoidance hypothesis. These predictions are subsequently tested in the SMChigh experiments (C96-C112), which support the predictions. The logical framework is sound and the predictions are clearly stated, making this a well-designed experimental approach to test the hypothesis.

results.result: Artificially increasing Smc levels 4-5 fold in SMChigh strains strongly impairs chromosome arm co-alignment with multiple parS sites but not with a single parS site. With two parS sites, SMChigh shows highly asymmetric alignment, visible paired-loop contacts, and hyper-enrichment of Smc between parS sites, consistent with increased collision frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C112 are strongly supported by immunoblotting, 3C-seq, and ChIP-seq data from SMChigh strains. The results directly confirm the predictions from C93-C95, showing that increased Smc levels cause organizational defects with multiple but not single parS sites. The rifampicin experiments (C106) strengthen the conclusion that Smc-Smc rather than Smc-RNA polymerase collisions are responsible. The similarity between Smc-CC425 and SMChigh phenotypes (C110-C111) supports a common mechanism of increased Smc flux leading to collisions.

results.result: Under physiological conditions, collisions between Smc-ScpAB complexes are kept at tolerable levels by fine-tuning multiple parameters: low cellular abundance (~30 Smc dimers per chromosome), high translocation rate, extended chromosome residency time, and preferential usage of clustered parS sites, possibly rendering collision resolution unnecessary.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C6, C113-C114 represent the main conclusion of the study, synthesizing evidence from all experimental approaches. The conclusion is well-supported by the collective data showing that perturbations to any of these parameters (arm modification, increased Smc levels, parS repositioning) lead to organizational defects. The inference that these parameters are fine-tuned to avoid collisions is reasonable, though the claim that collision resolution is unnecessary remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: Mild perturbations that increase collision frequency hamper chromosome organization, implying limited cellular capacity to resolve collisions. However, these organizational defects do not substantially impact bacterial growth, suggesting that chromosome segregation is efficiently supported even with collisions, though this may lead to cell-to-cell variations in chromosome organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C115-C118 are supported by the observation that various perturbations cause organizational defects visible by 3C-seq while maintaining normal or near-normal growth. The inference about limited collision resolution capacity is reasonable given that increased collision frequency leads to persistent defects. The speculation about cell-to-cell variation (C118) is logical but not directly tested in this study.

results.result: The authors propose that the parsimonious explanation is that Smc proteins cannot traverse one another, though they acknowledge that recent modeling studies suggest traversal may be needed to explain contact patterns. Direct observation of traversal and Z-loops in bacteria is lacking, and the molecular mechanism remains unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C129 present competing interpretations of the data. The authors favor a collision avoidance model without traversal (C123) as more parsimonious, while acknowledging that modeling studies (C124) suggest traversal may be necessary. The evaluation correctly notes the lack of direct experimental evidence for traversal (C125) and mechanistic understanding (C126, C129). This represents an honest assessment of uncertainty in the field, but the competing models are not definitively resolved by the presented data.

results.result: Most bacteria have clustered parS sites and are sensitive to their manipulation, while B. subtilis and related Bacilli have scattered parS sites, possibly serving a specialized function during sporulation when chromosome condensation at the origin rather than arm alignment may be beneficial.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C141 are primarily based on cited literature about parS distribution and function across bacteria, with speculative interpretation about the functional significance of scattered parS sites in B. subtilis. The citations support the observations about parS clustering in most bacteria and the phylogenetic restriction of scattered parS sites. The speculation about sporulation function (C138-C141) is reasonable given cited observations about chromosome organization during sporulation, though it remains untested.

results.result: Background claims establishing the known functions of SMC complexes, loop extrusion mechanisms, bacterial chromosome organization patterns, ParB-parS system, and the specific features of B. subtilis with eight scattered parS sites over ~0.75 Mb.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C27 represent established knowledge from the literature, properly cited and accurately described. These provide essential context for the study but are not novel findings. The characterization of B. subtilis parS distribution (C27) is an established feature of this organism shown in Figure 1A.

results.result: The presence of multiple types of SMC complexes on the same chromosome likely aggravates collision issues. In P. aeruginosa, a hierarchy exists where Smc-ScpAB limits MksBEF activity, possibly determined by relative abundance and chromosome association dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C122 are based on cited work in P. aeruginosa (Lioy et al., 2020). The inference about aggravated collisions with multiple SMC types (C119) is logical. The description of the hierarchy in P. aeruginosa (C120-C121) is supported by the cited literature. The proposed explanation for the hierarchy (C122) is speculative but reasonable.

results.result: The main conclusion that Smc DNA translocation is finely tuned to keep Smc encounter probability low, presumably enabling extensive DNA loop extrusion without requiring collision resolution mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claim C142 represents the overarching conclusion synthesizing all experimental findings. It is well-supported by the collective evidence from modified Smc proteins, parS site manipulations, and SMChigh experiments. The conclusion is appropriately cautious in using 'presumably' for the functional interpretation, acknowledging that while collision avoidance is demonstrated, the necessity of avoiding collision resolution remains somewhat inferential.
